mcqs.q: Periodontal instruments are classified according to:
opts: The metal from which the working end is cast
mcqs.explain: Carranza groups them as probes, explorers, scaling/root-planing/curettage instruments, endoscopes, and cleansing and polishing instruments — a functional classification.

mcqs.q: The three parts of a typical periodontal instrument are the:
mcqs.explain: Face, back and lateral side are parts of the blade itself, not of the whole instrument.

mcqs.q: A periodontal probe is used to locate, measure and mark pockets, and in addition to:
opts: Determine the configuration of the pocket
Polish the root surface after planing
mcqs.explain: Walking the probe around the tooth maps the shape of the pocket, not just its depth at one point.

mcqs.q: The typical periodontal probe is described as:
opts: A tapered, rodlike instrument calibrated in millimeters with a blunt, rounded tip
A triangular instrument with a flat face and a pointed tip
A spoon-shaped instrument with a rounded toe
A rigid instrument with a straight, chisel-like edge
mcqs.explain: The blunt rounded tip is essential — a sharp tip would perforate the junctional epithelium and give a false reading.

mcqs.q: Which probe has calibrations in 3-mm sections?
opts: The Michigan "O" probe with Williams markings
mcqs.explain: The Marquis is banded in alternating 3-mm colour blocks, which is why it is read in 3-mm increments.

mcqs.q: The UNC-15 probe is colour coded at which millimetres?
mcqs.explain: It is 15 mm long and marked at every millimetre, with colour coding only at 5, 10 and 15.

mcqs.q: The University of Michigan "O" probe with Williams markings is calibrated at:
mcqs.explain: The Williams pattern deliberately omits the 4 and 6 mm lines so the markings are easier to read apart.

mcqs.q: A 0.5-mm ball at the tip, markings at 3.5, 8.5 and 11.5 mm, and colour coding from 3.5 to 5.5 mm identify the:
mcqs.explain: The ball end and the 3.5–5.5 mm colour band are the features used for community index screening.

mcqs.q: The Nabers probe is specifically designed for:
opts: Measuring attachment loss on proximal surfaces
Screening a population for periodontal treatment need
mcqs.explain: Its curved working end follows the concavity between the roots, which a straight probe cannot enter.

mcqs.q: The Nabers probe carries colour-coded markings at:
mcqs.explain: The 3-mm intervals let horizontal furcation involvement be graded quickly.

mcqs.q: Explorers are used to locate calculus deposits and caries, and also to:
opts: Check the smoothness of the root surfaces after root planing
Measure the depth of the periodontal pocket
Remove the soft tissue lining of the pocket
Polish restorations at the gingival margin
mcqs.explain: Their fine point transmits the tactile sensation needed to confirm a glass-smooth root.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five basic scaling instruments?
mcqs.explain: The five are the curette, sickle, file, chisel and hoe; the explorer is a diagnostic instrument, not a scaling one.

mcqs.q: The sickle scaler is used primarily to remove:
opts: The soft tissue lining of the pocket
mcqs.explain: Its pointed tip makes it unsuitable for working below the gingival margin.

mcqs.q: The basic characteristics of a sickle scaler are:
opts: Triangular shape, double-cutting edge, pointed tip and flat surface
Curved spoon-shaped blade and a rounded toe
A single cutting edge offset at 60 degrees
A rigid straight blade with one bevelled end
mcqs.explain: The flat face and triangular cross-section give the sickle its two lateral cutting edges.

mcqs.q: Sickle scalers with CONTRA-ANGLED shanks are designed for:
mcqs.explain: Straight-shank sickles serve the anteriors and premolars; the contra-angle is what lets the blade reach around the posteriors.

mcqs.q: The curette is the instrument of choice for all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Removing the soft tissue lining of the periodontal pocket
mcqs.explain: Bulky supragingival deposits are the sickle's task; the curette's three classic indications are all at or below the gingival margin.

mcqs.q: Each working end of a curette has:
opts: A cutting edge on both sides of the blade and a rounded toe
A single cutting edge and a pointed tip
Two cutting edges meeting at a sharp point
A flat chisel edge across the end
mcqs.explain: The rounded toe, not a point, is what makes the curette safe in a deep pocket.

mcqs.q: Curettes can be adapted to deep pockets with minimal soft tissue trauma because they:
opts: Have no sharp points or corners other than the cutting edges of the blade
Are made of a softer alloy than sickle scalers
Are always used with a water spray
Have a shorter working end than sickle scalers
mcqs.explain: Being finer and free of sharp corners, the curette slides along the pocket wall instead of cutting it.

mcqs.q: The basic characteristics of a curette are:
opts: A curved (spoon-shaped) blade and a rounded tip
A triangular blade and a pointed tip
A flat face bevelled at 90 degrees with a straight edge
A rigid blade with a bi-bevelled cutting edge
mcqs.explain: This pair of features distinguishes it from the sickle at a glance.

mcqs.q: The straight design and pointed end of a sickle scaler can cause:
mcqs.explain: The point engages the pocket wall, whereas the curette's curved blade and rounded toe adapt to the root.

mcqs.q: Compared with the sickle, subgingival adaptation around the root is:
opts: Better with the sickle on facial surfaces only
mcqs.explain: The curved blade follows the convexity of the root around the line angles on both facial and lingual surfaces.

mcqs.q: The two basic types of curette are:
mcqs.explain: Gracey curettes are the classic area-specific set; Columbia #4R-4L is a classic universal.

mcqs.q: A universal curette can be inserted in most areas of the dentition by:
opts: Altering and adapting the finger rest, fulcrum and hand position of the operator
Changing the blade angle with a sharpening stone
Using it only with an ultrasonic handpiece
mcqs.explain: The instrument itself does not change — the operator's grip and fulcrum do.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a UNIVERSAL curette?
mcqs.explain: Younger-Good #7-8, McCall's #17-18 and Indiana University #17-18 are the other universals named in the lecture.

mcqs.q: Gracey curettes are probably the best instruments for subgingival scaling and root planing because they:
opts: Provide the best adaptation to complex root anatomy
Are the only curettes that can be sharpened
Have two usable cutting edges per blade
Are rigid enough to fracture heavy calculus
mcqs.explain: Each instrument in the set is angled for a particular region, so the blade meets the root correctly wherever it is used.

mcqs.q: Gracey #11-12 is designed for which surfaces?
mcqs.explain: #13-14 is the distal counterpart; #7-8 and #9-10 cover the posterior facial and lingual surfaces.

mcqs.q: Gracey #5-6 is designed for:
mcqs.explain: #1-2 and #3-4 are the purely anterior pair; #5-6 extends the range back as far as the premolars.

mcqs.q: A full set of SINGLE-ended Gracey curettes comprises how many instruments?
mcqs.explain: The same blades supplied double-ended make up the seven instruments 1/2 through 13/14.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the cutting edges is correct?
opts: The Gracey curette uses one cutting edge — the outer edge; the universal curette uses both
The Gracey curette uses both cutting edges; the universal uses only the outer edge
Both instruments use only the inner edge
Both instruments use both edges equally
mcqs.explain: The offset blade of the Gracey means only the lower, outer edge meets the tooth at the correct angle.

mcqs.q: The Gracey curette blade is:
opts: Curved in two planes — from shank to toe and also to the side
Curved in one plane — from shank to toe only
mcqs.explain: The universal curette has the simpler one-plane curvature, from shank toward the toe only.

mcqs.q: The face of the blade is bevelled at how many degrees to the shank in a GRACEY curette?
mcqs.explain: This is the offset blade; the universal curette's face sits at 90 degrees and is therefore not offset.

mcqs.q: An 'offset blade' describes which instrument?
mcqs.explain: Offset refers to the 60-degree bevel of the face relative to the terminal shank.

mcqs.q: Hoe, chisel and file scalers are used to remove:
opts: Tenacious subgingival calculus and altered cementum
The soft tissue wall of the pocket
mcqs.explain: Their use is limited compared with that of curettes, but they handle deposits a curette cannot shift.

mcqs.q: Instruments designed for use on implants and implant restorations are made of:
mcqs.explain: A harder, dissimilar metal would scratch the implant surface and create a plaque-retentive defect.

mcqs.q: Ultrasonic and sonic instruments are used for scaling and cleansing tooth surfaces and for:
opts: Curetting the soft tissue wall of the periodontal pocket
mcqs.explain: Chapter 52 of Carranza deals with sonic and ultrasonic instrumentation and irrigation together, for this reason.

mcqs.q: The magnification of a periodontal endoscope ranges from:
mcqs.explain: That range is enough to visualise even minute deposits of plaque and calculus within the pocket.

mcqs.q: The periodontal endoscope allows clear and deep visualization of:
mcqs.explain: It is an instrument for seeing inside the pocket, where conventional direct vision fails.

mcqs.q: Schwartz Periotrievers are:
opts: Highly magnetized instruments for retrieving a broken instrument tip
mcqs.explain: The long blade serves general use in pockets and the contra-angled tip is for furcations.

mcqs.q: On a Schwartz Periotriever, the contra-angled tip is intended for use in:
mcqs.explain: The long blade covers general use in pockets; the contra-angle reaches into the furcation.

mcqs.q: Compared with a sharp instrument, a dull instrument must be:
opts: Held more firmly and pressed harder
Held more lightly and drawn more slowly
Used only with an ultrasonic scaler
Used at a smaller blade-to-tooth angle
mcqs.explain: The extra grip and pressure reduce tactile sensitivity and increase the chance of an inadvertent slip.

mcqs.q: The objective of sharpening is to:
opts: Restore the fine, thin, linear cutting edge of the instrument
Reduce the blade angle from 90 to 60 degrees
Shorten the blade so it fits deeper pockets
Remove the bevel from the face of the blade
mcqs.explain: Sharpening must never distort the instrument's original angles — only restore the edge.

mcqs.q: The cutting edge of a DULL curette is:
mcqs.explain: When sharp, the junction of the face and lateral side is a fine line; wear rounds that junction off.

mcqs.q: Sharpening is performed by:
opts: Grinding the surfaces of the blade until their junction is once again sharply angular
Heating the blade and quenching it
Polishing the face of the blade with a rubber cup
Bending the terminal shank to restore the blade angle
mcqs.explain: The aim is a sharply angular junction rather than a rounded one, with the original angles preserved.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a sharpening stone listed in this lecture?
mcqs.explain: The four stones listed are flat India, flat Arkansas, cone-shaped Arkansas and ceramic; diamond sharpening cards are the other option shown.

mcqs.q: The cutting edge of a curette is formed at the junction of the:
mcqs.explain: Each blade therefore carries two cutting edges, one at each lateral side.

saqs.q: List the five groups into which periodontal instruments are classified according to the purposes they serve.
saqs.a: 1) Periodontal probes. 2) Explorers. 3) Scaling, root-planing and curettage instruments (sickle scalers; curettes; hoe, chisel and file scalers; implant instruments; ultrasonic and sonic instruments). 4) Periodontal endoscopes. 5) Cleansing and polishing instruments.

saqs.q: Name the three parts of a typical periodontal instrument and state the function of each.
saqs.a: The WORKING END is the part that contacts the tooth and performs the work (the blade). The SHANK connects the working end to the handle and determines the access the instrument has. The HANDLE is the part gripped by the operator.

saqs.q: Describe the five periodontal probes (A–E) together with their calibrations.
saqs.a: A — Marquis color-coded probe: calibrations in 3-mm sections. B — University of North Carolina 15 probe: 15 mm long, marked at each millimetre and colour coded at the 5th, 10th and 15th millimetres. C — University of Michigan "O" probe with Williams markings: at 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 10 mm. D — Michigan "O" probe: markings at 3, 6 and 8 mm. E — WHO probe: a 0.5-mm ball at the tip, markings at 3.5, 8.5 and 11.5 mm, and colour coding from 3.5 to 5.5 mm.

saqs.q: Compare the sickle scaler and the curette with respect to blade shape, tip, cutting edges and clinical use.
saqs.a: SICKLE — triangular in shape with a flat face, a double (two lateral) cutting edge and a POINTED tip; used primarily to remove supragingival calculus; its straight design and pointed end can lacerate and traumatise the soft tissue. CURETTE — curved, spoon-shaped blade with a cutting edge on both sides and a ROUNDED toe; finer than the sickle and with no sharp points or corners other than the cutting edges; the instrument of choice for deep subgingival calculus, root planing altered cementum, and removing the soft tissue lining of the pocket; it adapts better to the root subgingivally with minimal trauma.

saqs.q: Give the Gracey curette pairings and the area each pair serves.
saqs.a: #1-2 and #3-4 — anterior teeth. #5-6 — anterior teeth and premolars. #7-8 and #9-10 — posterior teeth, facial and lingual. #11-12 — posterior teeth, mesial. #13-14 — posterior teeth, distal. Single-ended Gracey curettes are also available, a full set comprising 14 instruments.

saqs.q: Tabulate the four differences between the Gracey (area-specific) and the universal curette.
saqs.a: AREA OF USE — Gracey: a set of many curettes designed for specific areas and surfaces; Universal: one curette designed for all areas and surfaces. CUTTING EDGE USE — Gracey: one cutting edge used, working with the outer edge only; Universal: both cutting edges used, working with either the outer or the inner edge. CURVATURE — Gracey: curved in two planes (blade curves from shank toward the toe and also appears to curve to the side); Universal: curved in one plane (from shank toward the toe only, not to the side). BLADE ANGLE — Gracey: offset blade, face bevelled at 60 degrees to the shank; Universal: blade not offset, face bevelled at 90 degrees to the shank.

saqs.q: Why are special instruments required for implants, and what are they made of?
saqs.a: Conventional stainless-steel scalers and curettes would scratch and roughen the implant surface, creating a plaque-retentive defect. Implant instruments are therefore plastic or titanium scalers and curettes designed for use on implants and implant restorations.

saqs.q: State the objective of instrument sharpening and explain why a sharp instrument is clinically preferable to a dull one.
saqs.a: OBJECTIVE: to restore the fine, thin, linear cutting edge of the instrument — accomplished by grinding the surfaces of the blade until their junction is once again sharply angular rather than rounded, and without distorting the original angles of the instrument. A sharp instrument cuts more precisely and quickly. A dull instrument must be held more firmly and pressed harder, which reduces tactile sensitivity and increases the possibility that the instrument will inadvertently slip.

saqs.q: Name the sharpening stones and cards illustrated in this lecture.
saqs.a: Sharpening stones: the flat India stone, the flat Arkansas stone, the cone-shaped Arkansas stone and the ceramic stone. In addition, diamond sharpening cards are used.

saqs.q: What are Schwartz Periotrievers and how are their two ends used?
saqs.a: They are highly magnetized instruments designed for retrieval of a broken instrument tip from the periodontal pockets and furcation. The long blade is for general use in pockets, and the contra-angled tip is for use in furcations.
